extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and practitioners in media economics, journalism studies, and media policy
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Napoli's audience-economics framework to understand and predict how news outlets choose stories given the dual-product marketplace (content for consumers and audiences for advertisers), measurement systems, and advertiser demands. Useful for analyzing newsworthiness, editorial incentives, and empirical modeling of story placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual-Product Marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Media firms produce content (sold to consumers) AND audiences (sold to advertisers). Selection optimizes simultaneously for: (a) attracting the desired audience demographic, AND (b) creating a measurable audience product to sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrammatic framing: media firms sit between a content market (consumers) and an audience market (advertisers) with audience-measurement firms mediating. News-selection logic responds to both markets; evaluate story choices by how well they perform on these two axes (consumer appeal and salability to advertisers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-Targeting Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that attract advertisers' target demographics (typically affluent adults 18–54) receive priority placement, even if alternative stories serve broader public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing news selection, account for advertiser-desired demo targets (e.g., affluent 18–54). Coverage may be skewed toward topics, frames, or sources that disproportionately appeal to those demographics because they increase ad revenue potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement Distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the measurement firm measures becomes the implicit operational definition of audience; un-measurable engagement is invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience-measurement firms (Nielsen, comScore, Chartbeat) do not merely report reality — their metrics become the operative reality for editorial and ad decisions. Evaluate how reliance on particular metrics can render certain forms of engagement (qualitative attention, offline sharing, long-tail interaction) invisible to decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicted-Audience-Size Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection optimizes against audience predictions; stories with predictably large audiences are favored over experimental coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial choices bias toward story types with predictable large reach. When modeling or critiquing news selection, include predicted-audience expectations as a selection variable; experimental or novel stories are disadvantaged because they threaten predictable audience returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic Stratification
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sections, programs, and time slots target different demographic clusters; story selection for each is filtered by target audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsworthiness relative to the specific demographic cluster served by a section/slot (e.g., morning show vs. late-night, business section vs. lifestyle). Segmentation means a story's value varies across outlet subsections and scheduling contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Quality over Audience Size
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller, affluent, attentive audiences command higher CPMs than larger, lower-income, fleeting audiences. Story selection is skewed toward attracting 'quality' audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ad-revenue calculations (CPM, targeting premiums) matter more than raw reach in some contexts. Evaluate selection incentives by anticipated ad price per unit of attention, not just by total audience size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-Subsidy Dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: News departments often subsidize entertainment programming (or vice versa); selection cycles reflect cross-subsidy economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming and story-choice decisions can be driven by internal budgetary trade-offs across divisions. When analyzing selection practices, consider how profitable/nonprofitable units subsidize others and how that shapes news priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Measurement Loop
rubrics_metrics.description: The iterative process: (1) Stories run. (2) Audience measurement firm reports demographics. (3) Advertisers buy/decline based on report. (4) Media firms adjust selection toward measurement-favorable demographics. (5) Future stories selected to optimize next measurement cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This loop is central: measurement both reflects and shapes content. Use this procedural sequence to trace causal pathways from metric design to editorial change; interventions at any step (measurement methods, advertiser reactions, editorial adjustments) will alter downstream selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Audience Marketplaces: Predicted vs Measured
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two audience marketplaces—predicted audience (editorial guesses about who will watch/read) and measured audience (actual realized audience post-publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The gap between predicted and measured audiences drives editorial learning: persistent under-prediction causes outlets to update toward higher-engagement story types. In evaluation, distinguish incentives tied to pre-publication predictions from those tied to ex-post measured outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daypart / Time-of-Day Differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different newsworthiness criteria operate at morning vs. evening vs. weekend slots based on which audience is likely to be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating story placement and prominence, account for the time-of-day audience mix; the same story may be promoted or deprioritized depending on daypart-specific advertiser and audience priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable-Topic Stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets cluster around topics with predictable audience response (sports, weather, lifestyle) for revenue stability; experimental topics struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability of audience response is a selection advantage. Research or critique should measure topical predictability and its correlation with coverage volume and placement; expect conservative topical portfolios in ad-dependent outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Niche-Audience Outlet Differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialty outlets (Bloomberg, ESPN, fashion magazines) serve niches with concentrated advertiser appeal; their newsworthiness criteria differ accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Niche outlets prioritize coverage that concentrates desirable advertiser-relevant audience attributes. Comparative evaluation should account for heterogeneity across outlets: what counts as newsworthy varies by niche advertiser demands and audience composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability for Empirical Modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlet-level demographic targets and ad-revenue dependencies can be used as covariates in story-placement models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napoli's framework is explicitly operationalizable: to test hypotheses about audience-driven selection, include measurable outlet characteristics (demographic targets, advertiser reliance, measurement system used) as independent variables in models of story placement, prominence, and topic choice.
